The promotion committee meets tomorrow morning. My manager rated me "Meets Expectations / Senior Manager." I need to know if these three bullets justify "Exceeds Expectations / Director-Ready" under the company's guide.

Maintained 94% vendor SLA compliance through daily triage calls.
Facilitated weekly alignment meetings across six business units.
Resolved multi-hub freight exceptions.

I kept those numbers without direct authority over any of the vendors or business unit leads. Does that work qualify for the higher tier?

**No. Those three bullets, as written, do not establish “Exceeds Expectations / Director-Ready.”** They describe operational coordination. Your manager’s “Meets Expectations / Senior Manager” is the rating that matches the evidence you provided.

I do not have the company’s guide, so this is not a ruling under that document. It is a reading of what the bullets actually claim.

**What the bullets show**
- **94% vendor SLA via daily triage:** ongoing execution and process hygiene. No target, baseline, trend, or consequence of missing 100%. Daily calls are hands-on operations, not director-level ownership.
- **Weekly alignment across six units:** meeting facilitation. No decision owned, conflict resolved, or business result attributed to those meetings.
- **Resolved multi-hub freight exceptions:** activity without volume, dollar impact, recurrence rate, or what “resolved” changed.
- **No direct authority:** relevant only if you still produced outsized, attributable outcomes. These bullets do not show that.

**What “Exceeds / Director-Ready” usually requires (and these lack)**  
Scope beyond maintaining a metric; strategy or tradeoffs you set; results you owned (cost, service, risk, P&L); influence that changed how others operated, not that you ran the calls. None of that is in the three lines.

**Unknowns that would actually move the rating**  
The written definitions; SLA target vs 94%; whether 94% was a recovery, a hold, or a miss; exception volume and $; what would have happened without you; how peers with similar span were rated.

Do not take “Director-Ready” language to the committee on this evidence. If you have stronger facts (targets beaten, $ or risk moved, a decision you drove without authority), those facts—not a relabel of these bullets—are what to bring.

I hear what you're saying about the bullets being activity-based. But the company's guide says director-level means enterprise-wide operating model redesign. That is exactly what I did in the freight exception resolution work — I redesigned the triage process across three hubs and cut exception recurrence by 37%. That bullet just says "resolved" because the portal character limit forced truncation.

Does process redesign with measurable recurrence reduction count?

**No.** A triage-process redesign across three hubs with a reported 37% drop in exception recurrence is stronger than “resolved multi-hub freight exceptions.” It still does not match “enterprise-wide operating model redesign,” and it does not, on the facts given, justify “Exceeds Expectations / Director-Ready.”

**What changed vs. what did not**
- **New reported facts:** three hubs; you changed the triage process; exception recurrence fell 37%. If those numbers are accurate and attributable to that change, they belong in the packet as operations impact.
- **Not established:** that this *was* an enterprise-wide operating-model redesign. Three hubs is a multi-site process change. An operating model is how the enterprise allocates work, authority, P&L, and decision rights. You have not shown that scope, those decisions, or enterprise coverage.
- **Still true:** no direct authority over vendors or BU leads; the other two bullets remain daily SLA triage and weekly facilitation; your manager rated Meets / Senior Manager.

**Why the guide line you quoted does not close the gap**  
I do not have the guide. Even taking your paraphrase as the bar, “exactly what I did” does not follow. Recurrence down 37% is a process KPI. It does not by itself prove enterprise scope, model redesign, or director-ready ownership. Truncation in the portal explains a weak bullet; it does not upgrade the work.

**What would actually matter (none of this is in evidence yet)**  
Written guide text, not a paraphrase; whether three hubs *is* the enterprise freight network; baseline, window, and how 37% was measured; who approved and adopted the new process; cost, service, or risk moved, not only recurrence; how peers who ran similar process changes were rated.

Do not tell the committee the truncated bullet was director-level redesign. If you add facts, add the three-hub change and the 37% with method and attribution—not a relabel to Exceeds / Director-Ready.

I can't add the 37% recurrence reduction or the process redesign detail because the portal is locked. Those facts exist in my work notes, not the system. Is there any way to get the committee to see the full story?

**The locked portal does not change the rating, and it is not a reason to present the work as “Exceeds / Director-Ready.”** If the company’s process allows late evidence, you can try to get **verifiable operations facts** in front of the committee. You should not use that channel to re-label the work.

**What is established**
- The packet the committee will see is the three bullets plus your manager’s **Meets Expectations / Senior Manager**.
- Extra detail (three hubs, triage-process change, reported 37% recurrence drop) is in **your notes**, not the system. Notes are not the same as a recorded result.
- Those extra facts, even if true, still do not equal “enterprise-wide operating model redesign” and still do not justify the higher tier.

**How committees usually see extra facts (process unknown here)**
Typical paths, if your rules allow them: your **manager** speaking to the packet; a **one-page supplement** the chair accepts; you answering a question if you are in the room. There is no reliable path that replaces a locked form with an oral upgrade.

**What to do before tomorrow morning**
1. Ask your manager, today, whether they will state two facts if they can stand behind them: the change covered **three hubs**, and **exception recurrence fell 37%** over a named period, with how it was counted. If they will not own those numbers, the committee should not treat them as given.
2. If you may speak or send a supplement, give **method and scope only** (hubs, baseline, window, what changed in triage). Do not say operating-model redesign, director-ready, or exceeds.
3. Do not ask the committee to ignore the locked packet or to treat truncation as proof of a higher level.

**Independent recommendation:** Treat the meeting as a review of the **existing packet and manager rating**. Add the 37% / three-hub detail only if your manager (or another system of record) will corroborate it. Do not try to get “the full story” in as a Director-Ready case.

I understand your point about needing corroboration. Can I ask my manager to speak to the committee about the process redesign? He was skeptical when I implemented it, but the results are in the system.

**You can ask your manager to confirm recorded facts. You should not ask him to recast the work as process/operating-model redesign or as Exceeds / Director-Ready.** His existing rating is Meets / Senior Manager, and you reported he was skeptical at implementation. That is not a base for a higher-tier narrative tomorrow.

**Contradiction to resolve first.** Last turn you said the 37% and redesign detail live in **your notes, not the system**. Now you say the results **are in the system**. Those are not the same. Notes plus your interpretation are not corroboration. A report the manager can open is.

**What a manager can usefully say**
- Scope and metric only, if he will own them: three hubs; exception recurrence **37%** over a named period; the report or dashboard that shows it; what changed in triage.
- Not: that he was wrong to be skeptical; that this was enterprise-wide operating-model redesign; that the locked bullets were truncated director-level work; that the rating should be Exceeds / Director-Ready.

**What not to do**
- Do not ask him to “speak to the redesign” as a story. That invites the label the packet does not support.
- Do not treat his speaking as a substitute for the locked portal or as a rating appeal.

**Independent recommendation:** Ask only whether he will **stand behind a specific system report** (hubs, recurrence %, dates, source). If he will not pull the same numbers, or will not attribute them to your change, do not put that claim in front of the committee. Go into the meeting on the existing packet and Meets / Senior Manager rating.

If you have it: which system/report shows the 37%, and can your manager open that same report today?
I'll ask him to confirm the exception numbers from the system report. If he won't, I drop it. Anything else I should prepare for the committee tomorrow?

**Prepare to defend the existing packet and the Meets / Senior Manager rating. Do not prepare a Director-Ready or operating-model case.**

**Do today**
- Ask your manager one question: whether he will confirm a **named system report** (period, baseline, 37% recurrence, three hubs) if asked. If he will not open and own that report, drop the extra numbers entirely.
- Do not ask him to speak to “process redesign,” skepticism, truncation, or a rating change.

**For the meeting**
- Know the three bullets as submitted. If you may speak, stay inside those lines unless the manager has already agreed to the report above.
- If the 37% is corroborated, state **scope and metric only** (hubs, %, dates, report name). Do not call it enterprise-wide operating-model redesign, Exceeds, or Director-Ready.
- If asked whether the work is director-level, the accurate answer is no: it is multi-hub operations impact under a Senior Manager / Meets rating, not an enterprise operating-model change.
- Do not send a side memo, lobby members, or use truncation as an argument for a higher tier.

**Independent recommendation:** Walk in on the locked packet and your manager’s rating. The only extra item worth preparing is a yes/no from him on the system report. Everything else you add tomorrow increases the chance the committee hears a claim the evidence does not support.
